This Murdered-Out Lamborghini Urus SE Looks Like a High-Riding Batmobile, Yours if You Want It
12 photos
Photo: Instagram | jesus.spec
Lamborghini may not care that much about the SE version of the Urus , because this model, just like the non-electrified S and Performante, not to mention the original pre-facelifted iteration, are dead and buried, and the sole-surviving Urus today is the SE Performante.
The latest iteration of the ultra popular (for an exotic) model was officially shown to the world earlier this year, and for whatever reason, it does not get that much attention. But that does not mean that it is a flop. Far from it, to be honest. It’s likely due to the fact that the Urus is not exactly a fresh model, even if the SE Performante is, because it has soldiered on with a few styling tweaks on the outside and some changes beneath the skin ever since 2017.
That is when the original Lamborghini Urus entered production at the Sant’Agata Bolognese factory in Italy, becoming the brand’s second most adventurous model ever after the LM002, aka the Rambo Lambo. And for what it’s worth, it was eventually joined by a third adventurous Raging Bull, namely the Huracan Sterrato , with its jacked-up design, and exclusive features inside and out and beneath the skin, which retired the brand’s previous-generation “baby” supercar.
Lamborghini’s new Urus SE Performante features a few stylistic tweaks on the outside, though they are discreet, so unless one is a fan or very familiar with this model, they might not be able to tell it apart from the demised variants. The most important upgrade lies beneath the skin, though, where the 4.0-liter twin-turbo V8 plug-in hybrid powertrain has been massaged to produce 801 hp (597 kW/812 ps) and 738 lb-ft (1,000 Nm) of torque combined.
Photo: Instagram | jesus.spec This makes it 12 hp (9 kW /12 ps) punchier than the old Urus SE , and 144 hp (107 kW/146 ps) more powerful than the S and Performante. This represents a 160 hp (119 kW/162 ps) boost over the original Urus. The model has a 194 mph (312 kph) top speed, needs 3.3 seconds to zip to 62 mph (100 kph), identical to the demised Urus Performante, and has a 37-mile (60 km) range on zero emissions.
With this short Lamborghini Urus history lesson behind us, it is now time to put the spotlight on the pictured vehicle, which is a brand new Urus SE. This machine has obviously been visited by the tuning fairy, as it has a murdered-out design. It has a satin black look on the outside, with a few glossy black elements here and there. The reflectors on the sides of the front bumper haven’t been darkened out, but the windows have.
There is no detail about the wheels, suspension, and other elements in the short caption on social media post embedded at the bottom of the page, which only reveals the model year, mileage, and asking price. It is a 2026 Lamborghini Urus SE that has 858 miles (1,381 km) under its belt, and it costs... Actually, we will leave this information away for now, revealing it toward the end of the story.
On the inside, the plug-in hybrid exotic crossover features light brown leather upholstery on the seats, parts of the dashboard panel, and door cards, with some white stitching for contrast. The Raging Bull’s logo is embroidered into the headrests. The pillars and headliner appear to have been wrapped in Alcantara in a hue similar to the leather upholstery, and a panoramic roof is also on deck, alongside the three main screens, and other features.
Photo: Instagram | jesus.spec With zero mods, the Lamborghini Urus SE hits 62 mph (100 kph) in 3.4 seconds, one-tenth of a second slower than its SE Performante predecessor, and has an identical top speed. Its plug-in hybrid twin-turbo V8 develops 789 hp (589 kW/800 ps) and 701 pound-feet (950 Nm) of torque. And given that this example is still brand new, it is likely that no horses have escaped the stable just yet.
A used Lamborghini Urus SE will typically set you back between $270,000 and almost $400,000 in today’s used car market in the New World. Therefore, one must have really deep pockets if they with to own such a thing. A nearly model year with quite a few miles under its belt can sometimes end up costing close to the $250,000 mark, whereas new examples can change hands for over $350,000 and sometimes close to the $400,000 mark, depending on the options.
Now that you know how much one of these usually retails for in today’s used car market on our shores, how much do you think the 2026 Lamborghini Urus SE, with its 858 miles, costs? The answer is $339,995. The vehicle is advertised on social media (Instagram) by @jesus.spec, and you know what to do if you really want it, right? But would you really blow $340K on this thing?
